title: Assignment: matrices, frequency, pointers and dynamic arrays
overview: These are Shammunul's answers to the assignment that follows the 2D-array and pointer modules. Each problem reuses one recent tool: a frequency array for counting, a matrix check with a flag, a pointer for a simple calculation, and `realloc` to grow an array one element at a time.

concepts.explain: Update `freq[value]++` as soon as you read each value. Then every later question is a single lookup.
First count every value. Then, on a second pass, count the elements whose frequency is 1.
Diagonal cells (`i == j`) must be 1 and every other cell must be 0. Keep the answer in a flag.
Subtract, then flip the sign if the result is negative. `abs(a - b)` from `<stdlib.h>` does the same.
Start with room for 1 element. Before storing element `i`, resize the block to `i + 1` elements.

files.title: Absolute difference using pointers
files.what: Reads `A` and `B` through pointers, subtracts, and makes the result positive.
steps: Read `A` and `B`, then point `ptr1` at `A` and `ptr2` at `B`.

files.title: Count occurrences in a matrix
files.what: Builds a frequency array while reading the matrix, then answers each query with `freq[x]`.
steps: Read the matrix, and add 1 to `freq[Numbers[i][j]]` for each cell.
files.complexity: Time O(N·M + X) · Space O(max value)
files.input_note: The sample: a 2×3 matrix, then 3 query numbers.
files.output_note: `2`, `1` and `0` (2 appears twice, 6 once and 7 never), which matches the expected answer.
files.watch_out: The queries are stored starting at index 1. That works because the array has spare room (`X + 5`), but storing from index 0 is less error-prone.

check.q: Why is `freq` sized 100005 when values are at most 1000?
check.a: It's just a safe upper bound. 1001 slots would be enough.

files.title: Count occurrences in a matrix (re-typed)
files.what: The same solution as `count_matrix.c`: count every matrix value in `freq` while reading, then answer each query with `freq[x]`. The queries are stored from index 0 this time.
steps: Read the matrix and do `freq[value]++` for every cell.
files.complexity: Time O(N·M + X) · Space O(N·M + max value)
files.input_note: The sample: a 2×3 matrix and the queries 2, 6 and 7.
files.output_note: `2`, `1`, `0`, the same as the original and the expected answer.

check.a: Only the query indexes: 0 to X-1 here, 1 to X there. The answers are identical.

files.title: Count numbers that appear only once
files.what: Counts every value, then counts the elements whose frequency is exactly 1.
steps: Second pass: add 1 to `count` for each element whose `freq` is 1.
files.output_note: `3`: the values 1, 5 and 6 appear once each.
files.watch_out: The second loop goes over the elements. That is only correct because a value with frequency 1 appears once in the array, so it is counted once.

files.title: Count numbers that appear only once (re-typed)
files.what: The same two passes as `no_repeatation.c`: count every value, then count the elements whose value has frequency 1.
steps: Pass 2: add 1 for every element with `freq[...] == 1`, then print the count.
files.complexity: Time O(N) · Space O(N + max value)

check.q: Would the answer change if pass 2 walked the values 1..10^5 instead of the elements?
check.a: No. Checking `freq[v] == 1` for every possible value counts each once-only value exactly once too.

files.title: Is it a unit matrix?
files.what: Checks that the diagonal cells are 1 and all other cells are 0, using a flag.
steps: For each cell: if `i == j`, it must be 1. Otherwise it must be 0. On a mismatch, set `flag = 0` and break out of the inner loop.
files.input_note: A 3×3 matrix with one stray 2 off the diagonal.

check.q: Is a 1×1 matrix `[1]` a unit matrix?
check.a: Yes, so the program prints YES.

files.title: Is it a unit matrix? (re-typed, no flag)
files.what: Same check as `unit_matrix.c`, but without a flag: the first wrong cell prints `NO` and `return 0;` ends the program on the spot.
steps: Walk every cell. On the diagonal (`i == j`) the value must be 1; elsewhere it must be 0.
At the first cell that breaks the rule, print `NO` and `return 0;`.
files.input_note: A 3×3 matrix with one stray 1 at row 1, column 2.
files.output_note: `NO`: cell (1,2) is off the diagonal but holds 1.
files.watch_out: `return 0;` inside `main` ends the whole program, so it leaves both loops at once. That is why no flag and no second `break` are needed here.

check.q: Why doesn't this version need a `flag` variable?
check.a: It never has to remember the result: it prints NO and stops at the first bad cell, so reaching the end means every cell was fine.

files.title: Grow an array one element at a time
files.what: Starts with a 1-element block and uses `realloc` to make room for each new number before storing it.
steps: For each `i`: read the number into `num_array[i]`.
Call `realloc(arr, (i + 1) * sizeof(int))` so there is room for `i + 1` values, then store `arr[i]`.
files.complexity: Time O(N) on average (each `realloc` may copy) · Space O(N)
files.watch_out: `num_array` is an extra fixed-size array that isn't needed. Read into a plain `int x`. Also check whether `realloc` returned `NULL`.

check.q: On the first iteration (i = 0), how big does `realloc` make the block?
check.a: 1 int, the same size as before.

files.title: Grow an array one element at a time (re-typed)
files.what: The same program as `dynamic_array.c`: start with `malloc` room for one int and `realloc` to `i + 1` ints each time a number is read.
steps: For each number: read it, `realloc` to `(i+1)*sizeof(int)`, and store it in `arr[i]`.
files.complexity: Time O(N²) worst case (each realloc may copy) · Space O(N)
files.output_note: `1 4 2 6 9`, in the order they were read.
files.watch_out: As in the original, `num_array` isn't needed: reading into a plain `int x` and storing `arr[i] = x` does the same job.

check.q: What does `realloc` do with the numbers already in the block when it has to move it?
check.a: It copies them into the new, bigger block and frees the old one, so the values are kept.

recap: Build a frequency array once, then answer many count questions instantly.
Unit matrix: 1 on the diagonal and 0 everywhere else. Use a flag to check it.
`realloc` lets an array grow as input arrives.
Absolute difference: subtract, then flip the sign if the result is negative.

check_yourself.q: How would you find the value that appears most often, using a frequency array?
check_yourself.a: Count everything, then scan `freq` and keep track of the index with the largest count.

check_yourself.q: Why is it a bad idea to write `arr = realloc(arr, ...)` without checking the result?
check_yourself.a: If `realloc` fails, it returns NULL. That overwrites your only pointer to the old block, so the memory is lost.

body: This is an assignment day, so there is nothing new to learn on this page. Five problems, and each one picks up a tool from the last three modules: a frequency array for counting, a matrix walked with nested loops and a flag, a pointer, and `realloc` for an array that grows as the input arrives.
The work on a day like this is recognising which tool a problem is asking for. Below is a one-paragraph reminder of each, with a tiny example.
**Counting.** The tally sheet from Module 13: the value itself picks the slot. Take the six numbers `1 4 3 3 5 4` and do `freq[x]++` as you read each one.

Now every counting question is one lookup instead of a search. "How many 3s?" is `freq[3]`, which is 2. "How many values appear exactly once?" is a second walk over the numbers, counting those whose `freq` is 1, and here that is 1 and 5, so the answer is 2. Watch the size: make the tally as big as the largest value the problem allows, not as big as `N`.
This does not change when the numbers arrive in a grid instead of a line. A matrix cell is just another number, so tick `freq[a[i][j]]++` while you read the matrix, and answer the queries afterwards.

**Checking a matrix.** Two loops over every cell, and one flag holding the answer. Start at `flag = 1`, meaning "true so far", and clear it on the first cell that breaks the rule. For a unit matrix the rule is: on the diagonal (`i == j`) the cell must be 1, everywhere else it must be 0.

Watch out for two things here. A `break` inside the inner loop only leaves the inner loop, so the outer one keeps running; the answer is still right, but nothing is saved. And the rows and columns count from 0, so cell (2,1) is the second column of the third row.
intro.trace:
1 0 0    i==j -> must be 1  ok
0 1 0    others -> must be 0  ok
0 2 1    (2,1) is 2, not 0   -> NO

body: **Pointers.** A pointer holds an address, and the star follows it. After `int *ptr1 = &A;` the expression `*ptr1` is `A` itself, so `*ptr1 - *ptr2` is the same subtraction you would write with plain `A - B`. For an absolute difference, subtract and then flip the sign if the result came out negative.

**Growing an array.** Ask for one element with `malloc(sizeof(int))`, then before storing element `i`, resize the block so it has room for `i + 1` values. `realloc` keeps everything already in the block, so the earlier numbers survive each step:

Assign the result of `realloc` back to the pointer, because the block may have been moved to a new address. On a judge, none of these five problems is hard once it has been matched to its tool; what costs marks is the small print. Size the frequency array from the stated limits, count matrix indexes from 0, and print exactly what is asked, such as `YES` or `NO` in capitals and one answer per line.
The programs below are Shammunul's answers, each shown with the input it was run on and with the awkward parts noted.
